items.title: Rayzon Solar to start 5.1 GW TOPCon cells in Dec; proposes 5.1 GW ingot-wafer by 2028
items.text: Gujarat-based Rayzon Solar (unlisted) said cell production at its 5.1 GW TOPCon facility begins in December 2026, with first deliveries in Q1 2027. It also proposes 5.1 GW of ingot casting and wafer slicing by 2028; capex is undisclosed and the site is not finalised as it talks to several states about incentives. It adds to the ingot-wafer pipeline ahead of ALMM List-III, though it remains a proposal.

items.title: Jakson Group plans 10 GW ingot-wafer, 5 GW cell complex in Andhra Pradesh (Rs 6,863 cr)
items.text: Solar Now (republishing SOLARbytes) reports Jakson Group plans an investment of INR 6,863 crore for 10 GW of silicon ingots and wafers and 5 GW of solar cells on 290 acres at Meedivemula, Kurnool district. Phase 1 (3 GW ingot-wafer, 3 GW cells) is to start commercial production in May 2028; the rest by 2030. The State Investment Promotion Board has only recommended the land allotment, so this is not final. It adds another unlisted entrant to the ingot-wafer pipeline, raising oversupply and utilisation risk for listed peers.

items.title: Waaree Q2 FY27: revenue +23.9% to Rs 7,518 cr, PAT -14.2%; order book Rs 59,200 cr
items.text: Waaree Energies reported Q2 FY27 revenue of Rs 75.18 billion, up 23.9% year on year, while profit after tax fell 14.2% to Rs 7.54 billion. Operating EBITDA fell 5.1% to Rs 13.35 billion and the margin narrowed to 17.8% from 23.2%. The order book was about Rs 592 billion as of 26 Oct 2026, including 25.6 GW of module orders. The company is still developing its 10 GW ingot-wafer facility at Nagpur, and the article gives no new timeline. Margin pressure while it funds upstream capex is the point to watch.

items.title: China's draft export curbs on 12 solar technologies: licensing seen delaying Indian ingot-wafer capex
items.text: China's Joint Announcement No. 48 (issued 16 Oct 2026; consultation closes 15 Nov 2026) covers 12 solar technologies. Prohibited items include fluidised-bed polysilicon and wafers no thicker than 70 micrometres; licensed items include large polysilicon plant engineering, advanced crystal pulling, wafer cutting and TOPCon/HJT/XBC cell processes. A temporary pre-export registration requirement is already in force. A full ban is seen as unlikely, but licensing and longer lead times could raise capex and delay new plants, with Premier Energies' Rajesh Rustagi expecting limited initial impact.

items.title: IEEFA/JMK: India module capacity ~7x cell and ~116x ingot-wafer capacity; utilisation 35-40%
items.text: An IEEFA analysis modelled by JMK Research, reposted 23 Oct 2026, puts India's module capacity at about 233 GW by June 2026, roughly 7x cell capacity and 116x ingot-wafer capacity. Module makers run at about 35-40% utilisation versus the 50-65% needed for sustainable operations, with about 135 GW more module capacity firmly committed. It underlines the upstream gap that ALMM List-III is meant to close, but also the overcapacity risk for module-heavy listed makers.

items.title: JM Financial: China's proposed solar tech export curbs could speed India's wafer push
items.text: China's commerce and science ministries proposed on 16 Oct adding 12 solar PV manufacturing technologies (polysilicon, wafers, cells and related equipment) to its prohibited/restricted export catalogue; feedback is open until 15 Nov 2026. JM Financial called it structurally positive for Indian manufacturing and said the greatest opportunity lies upstream, but warned of near-term disruption since India depends on China for equipment, gases, chemicals and engineers. It added that India may relax the ALMM-II mandate beyond December 2026 if domestic prices rise sharply.

items.title: Agastya Energy CEO flags utilisation risk as India ingot-wafer capacity heads to ~80 GW
items.text: In a Mercom interview, Agastya Energy CEO Bernhard Rack said India's ingot and wafer capacity is projected at about 80 GW by June 2028 against ALMM List-III's 15 GW threshold. A 12 GW plant needs roughly 80-85% utilisation to be globally competitive; at 60%, fixed cost per watt is about 50% higher. He noted 200+ GW of module capacity runs at about 35-40% utilisation, a caution for listed names building multi-GW wafer plants.
